newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ seeks Antarctic environment action, 1999 meeting.
newsitem.headline: NZ seeks Antarctic environment action, 1999 meeting.

text.p: New Zealand's Prime Minister Jim Bolger has called on nations with an interest in the future of the Antarctic to join in protecting its fragile environment and proposed a ministerial gathering be held on edge of the frozen continent.

Addressing delegates to the 21st Antarctic Treaty Consultative Meeting in the southern city of Christchurch, Bolger said New Zealand was concerned about the ease of access to the frozen continent as well as pressures on its resources.
"New developments, such as air navigation services, will draw Antarctica more and more into the global village," he said in a speech delivered on Monday evening.
"That is why New Zealand holds in such high regard the establishment of the Committee for Environmental Protection (CEP)."
Officials said on Tuesday that the committee was now likely to come into existence this year as Japan and Russia had indicated they would ratify necessary protocols by December.

Bolger urged representatives of 43 participant states to look for new policies that would ensure "responsive stewardship" of the polar area. He also suggested a ministerial meeting on Ross Island, Antarctica, in early 1999.

"1999 marks the 40th anniversary of the Antarctic Treaty. We should mark this occasion in a way that befits the treaty and sends a signal to the world that we intend to nurture and strengthen it through the 21st century," he explained.

Bolger said he hoped to be able to invite ministers from the inner circle of 26 consultative parties to meet on the island, where New Zealand and the U.S. both have key scientific stations, in January or February 1999.
New Zealand's senior official at the conference, Stuart Prior, estimated this could involve a visit by about 60 people to the mountainous island on the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf.
Part of Wellington's political concern, expressed in its role as host of the meetings which run until Friday, is that states are losing their collective bite on environmental issues.

In part, this worry centres on delays by Japan and Russia in formally ratifying the 1991 Madrid Protocol -- a supplement to the Antarctic Treaty setting out environmental protection rules for land areas -- which has postponed the creation of a CEP.
The Madrid accord covers waste disposal, marine pollution and the conservation of plants and wildlife, and aims to protect the wilderness from exploitation.

More live at the moment, however, is anger at the way that the Convention for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR) is being blatantly challenged by the plunder of valuable toothfish by pirate fishing in Antarctic waters.
Bolger said New Zealand was "seriously concerned" and would liaise with its convention partners "to take appropriate steps to prevent a 'free-for-all' in the Southern Ocean".
